title: Truthiness vs bool, if and match

answers: The branches produce different types: an integer and a `&str`
`if` cannot appear on the right-hand side of `let`
writing.exampleCaption: `match` with a range covers every `u32`, and the `if` expression yields a `&str` from either branch.
writing.explanation:
`if (!count)` mixes several questions: is it `0`, `NaN`, `""`, `null` or `undefined`? Rust refuses to guess. `if count` with an integer is E0308, expected `bool`, found integer, so you write the question you mean: `count == 0`, `text.is_empty()`, `value.is_none()`. There is no `==` versus `===` either. `==` compares two values of compatible types through `PartialEq` and never converts, so `0 == ""` does not compile.

`if` is an expression, which replaces both the statement form and the ternary. `let urgent = if count > 0 && count < 5 { "yes" } else { "no" };` works because both branches are `&str`. If one branch yields a number and the other text, the expression has no single type and rustc rejects it. An `if` without `else` has type `()`, so it can only stand as a statement.

`match` is the tool for several cases of one value. Patterns can be literals, ranges such as `1..=4`, or `_` for everything else, and the compiler checks that the arms cover every possible value. For a `u32`, the arms `0`, `1..=4` and `_` are exhaustive, so no input can fall through, unlike a `switch` without `default`.

`&&` and `||` short-circuit as in JavaScript, but they accept and return only `bool`. There is no `a || b` default trick; that job belongs to `Option` methods such as `unwrap_or`, covered in the lesson on `null` and `undefined`.
writing.feedback: An `if` expression has one type. Return `count.to_string()` from the first branch and `String::from("none")` from the second, or a number from both.
writing.question: Why does `let label = if count > 0 { count } else { "none" };` not compile?

recall.answer: E0308: the condition must be a `bool`, and a `String` is not one. Ask the exact question, such as `if !name.is_empty()`. Rust never converts a string, a number or an `Option` to a boolean.
recall.question: What is the error, and what is the fix?

recall.answer: `100..=255`. rustc rejects the `match` with E0004 and names that range. Add an arm for it or a `_` arm: a `match` must cover every value of the type.
recall.question: Which values of `n: u8` are not covered by this `match`?

writing.rule: `if` requires a `bool`, and every branch of an `if` or `match` expression must produce the same type.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness passes every case, including `0` and exactly `100`. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.summary: Rust has no truthy or falsy values: a condition must be a `bool`, and `if` and `match` are expressions whose branches share one type.
